question: to the Commission Alvise Pérez (NI) Subject:

Europe is facing a decisive industrial transformation. While China and the United States are making strides in artificial intelligence, robotics, digital platforms and software-defined vehicles, much of European industry remains stuck in a 20th century model: namely powerful factories with limited in-house capabilities for coding, data management, automation and digital integration. The German case is particularly worrying. Germany, the EU’s industrial powerhouse, ranks only mid-table in terms of digitalisation and lags far behind in digital administration. In the automotive sector, Volkswagen’s need to partner with Rivian or XPeng highlights that even Europe’s major industrial champions are increasingly reliant on third parties for critical software technologies. Industrial strength in the 21st century is no longer decided solely by assembly lines, but by AI, operating systems, data, chips, the cloud, robotics and speed of execution. This technology lag will not be resolved by more abstract public plans, but rather by unlocking private investment, reducing energy costs, simplifying regulations and allowing European companies to compete. 1.
Does the Commission recognise that this technology lag in terms of software, AI and digitalisation threatens the EU’s industrial competitiveness?
Will the Commission assess the cumulative impact of bureaucracy, regulation and energy costs on investment in technology in the EU?
What specific measures will it take to accelerate private investment, regulatory simplification and digital industrialisation in the EU?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (4.9.2026) The Commission agrees on the need for substantial investment in critical digital technologies for the EU’s competitiveness. A clear-eyed assessment of the EU’s reliance on foreign software, products, AI models and digital infrastructure is the starting point of the recent Communication on Tech Sovereignty Package1, designed to boost the EU’s capacity to develop and deploy such technologies and curb strategic dependencies that affect competitiveness. The Strategic Roadmap for Digitalisation and AI in the Energy Sector2 advocates for a digitalised, interconnected energy system increasing electrification and clean energy integration to face high energy prices. The package also calls for the urgent mobilisation of private risk capital to address the gap in high-risk financing for EU deep-tech firms and large-scale infrastructure, against investment need estimated more broadly at up to EUR 450 billion by 2036, and the injection of considerable resources into strategic technologies by other economies. In parallel, the Commission is looking to increase AI uptake in EU strategic sectors through the AI Continent Action Plan3 and the Apply AI Strategy4. It is also undertaking a regulatory ‘deep cleaning’ as part of the Digital Simplification Package5. The AI Omnibus clarifies the application timelines of the AI Act6, and the proposal for a Digital Omnibus aims to unlock data and provide legal certainty for AI training. To gauge the cumulative impact of digital rules, the 2027 Digital Fitness Check7 will assess whether governance delivers a predictable, harmonised rulebook.
1 COM(2026) 503. 2 COM(2026) 501. 3 COM(2025) 165. 4 COM(2025) 723. 5 COM(2025) 837. 6 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down

harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act). 7 https://ec.europa.eu/info/law/better-regulation/have-your-say/initiatives/15554-Digital-fitness-check-testing-thecumulative-impact-of-the-EUs-digital-rules_en.
